hero.title: Cold, under control.

problem.title: An ice pack stops at 0 °C.
problem.body: Ice cream, frozen desserts and small frozen goods are moving from central warehouses and long hauls to 30–90 minute delivery from stores and dark stores. The tool doing the job is still mostly an ice pack: it stays near 0 °C, many are thrown away after a single run, and none of them can tell you what the temperature did along the way.

items.title: Not cold enough
items.body: Ordinary ice packs stay near 0 °C. Frozen desserts and frozen goods need a colder, controllable range.

items.title: Cooling you can't dose
items.body: Ice is added by guesswork: too much in summer, wasted in winter. Loose dry ice over-cools whatever touches it.

items.title: Nothing you can see
items.body: No temperature reading, no CO₂ reading, nothing to trace quality back to.

control.title: The fan is the throttle.
control.body: Dry ice never blows onto the food. Return air from the food zone passes through the single 120 × 120 mm PWM fan and the aluminium fins, hands its heat to the dry-ice chamber, and flows back into the box. A faster fan mean stronger heat exchange and faster pull-down; a slower fan mean gentler convection, slower dry-ice use and no local over-cooling. Every 2 seconds the controller reads three temperature channels, averages the valid ones, and runs PID to set the next fan PWM. This logic is written into the V1 firmware and passes host-side replay tests; how well it holds temperature on real hardware is still to be measured.

co2.title: CO₂ alarm threshold demo
co2.steady: Alarm on (shown steady in reduced-motion mode)
co2.rule: Firmware rule: ≥ 2000 ppm for about 3 seconds triggers the alarm; at ≥ 5000 ppm it blinks faster. Once triggered, the alarm clears only on a valid reading below 2000 ppm. Sensor range 0–5000 ppm.

safety.volume: 1 kg of dry ice sublimates into roughly 0.5 m³ of CO₂ (order-of-magnitude estimate, not measured).
safety.warning: Do not use in closed vehicles, rooms or poorly ventilated spaces.
facts: Food air, CO₂ exhaust and wiring never share a path
Always-open primary vent plus an always-open backup; venting continues with power off or fan stopped
The ePTFE membrane only keeps out dust and splashes; the dry-ice chamber is never a pressure vessel
Sensor range 0–5000 ppm; ≥ 2000 ppm for about 3 s raises the alarm

companyIntro.title: Turning cold-chain cooling from a consumable into a system.
companyIntro.body: Effi-Chillcrate X1 focuses on controllable dry-ice cold chain for rapid delivery. We are starting with a V1 lid that fits a 33 L cooler, bringing dry ice, heat exchange, fan control and CO₂ venting into one testable product system.

solutions.title: A complete system for short-distance delivery that needs low temperatures.
solutions.body: From the cold end to the delivery context, Effi-Chillcrate X1 connects product structure, control logic and safety boundaries in one product path.

items.title: Controllable cold
items.body: The target range can be set and fan PWM responds to temperature feedback. Pull-down speed, uniformity and hold time remain to be tested.

items.title: Reusable platform
items.body: The 33 L cooler body stays in place while the functional lid is upgraded; routine replenishment is dry ice and verified consumables.

items.title: Visible safety
items.body: Food air, CO₂ exhaust and electrical signals stay separate, with temperature and CO₂ status designed to be visible.

newsInfo.title: News & cold-chain knowledge
newsInfo.body: Verified reports and practical guidance on temperature control, food safety and dry ice.

news.title: UNEP and FAO publish sustainable food cold-chain report
news.summary: The report estimates that 14% of food produced for human consumption is lost in supply chains, highlighting the value of effective cold chains.

news.title: CDC: vaccines require controlled temperatures in transit
news.summary: CDC guidance specifies suitable containers, continuous temperature monitoring and transport logs. Ordinary food coolers are not qualified vaccine transport containers.

news.title: Cold-chain packaging moves toward reuse and material reduction
news.summary: BioPharma Dive cites Cryopak industry estimates of 4.5–5.0 million metric tons of EPS packaging entering the market annually, with roughly 1.2–1.5 million metric tons recycled. The estimate varies by region and product.

news.title: UNEP and IIR release three cold-chain technology briefs
news.summary: The briefs cover fishing vessels, walk-in cold rooms and commercial and domestic refrigeration, with practical guidance on food-loss reduction, energy efficiency, refrigerants and foam blowing agents.

news.title: Polyurethane recycling still faces material and flame-retardant limits
news.summary: A 2025 systematic review describes mechanical, chemical and thermal-recycling routes for polyurethane, while noting that additives and product context affect treatment difficulty. One study should not be generalized to every PU cooler.

news.title: Why use dry ice for some frozen shipments?
news.summary: Dry ice sublimates at about −78.5 °C without leaving meltwater, which can reduce moisture and some disposable ice-pack use. It is not a universal solution: packaging compatibility, ventilation and product temperature rules still apply.

news.title: Dry ice and sustainability: less packaging waste is not zero carbon
news.summary: Dry ice can use CO₂ captured from industrial processes and leaves no meltwater. Suitable disposable-coolant substitution and reusable containers may reduce consumables. Dry ice is a coolant; EPS, PU and vacuum panels are insulation, so they are not interchangeable. Captured CO₂ is ultimately released, and environmental comparisons require production, transport, reuse and food-loss data.

news.title: Seafood safety: temperature and cross-contamination
news.summary: FDA recommends separating raw and cooked seafood, cleaning coolers and keeping lids closed. Freezing does not kill all harmful germs.

faq.q: Why do food and medical samples need different handling?
faq.a: Their temperature ranges, packaging and records differ. The equipment capability shown here is general; each route needs a product-specific plan.

faq.q: Why is independent exhaust important with dry ice?
faq.a: Sublimated dry ice produces carbon dioxide. Independent exhaust keeps it out of the food-air loop, while the surrounding area still needs ventilation.
No. Refrigerated and frozen cargo have different requirements. Follow the specific product instructions and allow space for packaging and airflow.
